questions.q: Define the minor \(M_{23}\) and cofactor \(A_{23}\) of the element 6 in the determinant \(\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8 & 9 \end{vmatrix}\). Write the exact \(2 \times 2\) determinant for \(M_{23}\) and state the sign factor for \(A_{23}\).
questions.a: \(M_{23} = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 7 & 8 \end{vmatrix} = (1)(8) - (2)(7) = 8 - 14 = -6\). Since element 6 is at position (2,3), \(i+j = 5\) (odd), so \(A_{23} = (-1)^5 M_{23} = -(-6) = 6\). A wrong answer like \(M_{23} = \begin{vmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 7 & 8 \end{vmatrix}\) reveals the student deletes the wrong row/column (keeps row 2 instead of deleting it). A sign error (writing \(A_{23} = -6\)) reveals confusion about whether \((-1)^{i+j}\) uses 1-based or 0-based indexing.

questions.q: Explain why the determinant \(\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8 & 9 \end{vmatrix}\) expands to the same value whether you use Row 1 or Row 2, but the sum \(a_{11}A_{21} + a_{12}A_{22} + a_{13}A_{23}\) equals zero. Use the concept of identical rows in your explanation.
questions.a: Expanding along Row 1 gives \(\Delta = a_{11}A_{11} + a_{12}A_{12} + a_{13}A_{13}\). Expanding along Row 2 gives \(\Delta = a_{21}A_{21} + a_{22}A_{22} + a_{23}A_{23}\). Both equal the same determinant value by theorem. However, \(a_{11}A_{21} + a_{12}A_{22} + a_{13}A_{23}\) is the expansion of a determinant where Row 1 is replaced by Row 1 again (i.e., two identical rows), which must be zero. A student who says "it's zero because cofactors are different" misses the structural reason: it's exactly the determinant of a matrix with two identical rows, which is always zero by Property 3 of determinants.

questions.q: Evaluate the determinant \(\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & -3 & 5 \\ 6 & 0 & 4 \\ 1 & 5 & -7 \end{vmatrix}\) by expanding along the second row. Show all minors, cofactors, and the final computation.

Given \(\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} a & b & c \\ d & e & f \\ g & h & i \end{vmatrix}\), a student claims that \(a A_{11} + b A_{12} + c A_{13} = d A_{11} + e A_{12} + f A_{13}\) because both equal \(\Delta\). Analyze this claim and identify the exact error.
questions.a: The claim is false. The first sum \(a A_{11} + b A_{12} + c A_{13}\) is the cofactor expansion along Row 1, which equals \(\Delta\). The second sum \(d A_{11} + e A_{12} + f A_{13}\) uses Row 2 elements with Row 1 cofactors — this is the expansion of a determinant where Row 1 is repeated (Row 2 replaces Row 1 but cofactors still come from Row 1), so it equals 0, not \(\Delta\). The error is confusing "cofactor of element in Row 1" with "cofactor used in Row 1 expansion". Cofactors \(A_{1j}\) are tied to Row 1 positions; multiplying Row 2 elements by Row 1 cofactors creates a determinant with two identical rows.

questions.q: A student evaluates \(\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 & 4 \end{vmatrix}\) by expanding along Column 2 and writes: \(M_{12} = \begin{vmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \end{vmatrix} = -6\), \(A_{12} = -6\); \(M_{22} = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{vmatrix} = 0\), \(A_{22} = 0\); \(M_{32} = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 3\), \(A_{32} = 3\). Then computes \(\Delta = 0(-6) + 3(0) + (-2)(3) = -6\). Is this correct? If not, find the error.
questions.a: The answer is incorrect. The cofactor signs are wrong: \(A_{12} = (-1)^{1+2} M_{12} = -(-6) = 6\) (not \(-6\)). \(A_{32} = (-1)^{3+2} M_{32} = -(3) = -3\) (not \(3\)). Correct expansion: \(\Delta = 0(6) + 3(0) + (-2)(-3) = 6\). The student applied the sign pattern incorrectly — they likely used a fixed sign for the column instead of \((-1)^{i+j}\). This is a classic "sign convention" error that costs marks in both board and JEE exams.

questions.q: Construct a \(3 \times 3\) determinant with integer entries such that: (a) expanding along Row 1 requires computing three non-zero \(2 \times 2\) minors, (b) expanding along Column 3 requires only one non-zero minor, and (c) the determinant value is 12. Provide the matrix and verify both expansions.
questions.a:
One example: \(A = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & 4 & 0 \\ 5 & 6 & 3 \end{vmatrix}\).
Row 1 expansion: \(M_{11} = \begin{vmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 6 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = 12\), \(A_{11}=12\); \(M_{12} = \begin{vmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 5 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = 9\), \(A_{12}=-9\); \(M_{13} = \begin{vmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ 5 & 6 \end{vmatrix} = -2\), \(A_{13}=-2\). \(\Delta = 1(12) + 2(-9) + 0(-2) = 12 - 18 = -6\) — not 12. Need to adjust.
Better: \(A = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix}\).
Column 3: only \(a_{33}=2\) non-zero. \(M_{33} = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = 6\), \(A_{33}=6\). \(\Delta = 2(6)=12\).
Row 1: \(M_{11}=6, A_{11}=6\); \(M_{12}=0, A_{12}=0\); \(M_{13}=0, A_{13}=0\). \(\Delta = 2(6)+1(0)+0(0)=12\).
Row 1 actually has two zero minors here. To satisfy (a) strictly: \(A = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 \end{vmatrix}\) (no zeros, but Col 3 expansion still has three non-zero minors). The point is to test if student understands strategic choice of row/column. A good answer shows any matrix meeting criteria and verifies both expansions yield 12.
